raw_sentence: Q: How do you get rid of Adderall tongue?
raw_line: Q: How do you get rid of Adderall tongue? A: Adderall tongue is a common side effect of Adderall that can detrimentally and seriously affect a person’s quality of life. To help relieve Adderall tongue stay well-hydrated. Adderall and other ADHD medications can cause dehydration, so you need to drink at least 6 to 8 glasses of fluid per day. Take frequent sips of water rather than drinking a whole glass of water at once. Use artificial saliva products (such as sprays or lozenges) – these can help moisten the tissue and last longer than water. There are many different brands of these available over the counter at drug stores and they can be used multiple times a day. Chew sugar-free gum or suck on sugar-free candy – this contains xylitol which increases salivary flow and can help prevent dental decay. Avoid sucking candy that contains sugar because this will increase your risk of dental decay

raw_sentence: Q: Why does Lexapro (escitalopram) cause weight gain?
raw_line: Q: Why does Lexapro (escitalopram) cause weight gain? Complete Patient Guide A: Lexapro weight gain affects up 25 % to 41% of patients who take this antidepressant medication, although weight gain tends to be minimal, with an average gain of approximately 1 % to 3.7%. The weight gain associated with Lexapro occurs primarily due to the drug's mechanism of action on serotonin levels in the brain. When Lexapro blocks the serotonin transporter, it successfully increases serotonin availability to help treat depression and anxiety, but this same action can trigger unwanted changes in appetite and metabolism.

raw_line: Q: Is famotidine safer than omeprazole for heartburn? A: For most people with mild, occasional heartburn, famotidine is usually the safer first choice because it works quickly, can be taken as needed, and has fewer long‑term safety concerns than omeprazole. raw_sentence: Q: Can you take ibuprofen on an empty stomach?
raw_line: Q: Can you take ibuprofen on an empty stomach? A: Despite the common belief that you must take ibuprofen with food, you can safely take low-dose ibuprofen (up to 1200 mg daily in divided doses for 1 to 7 days) on an empty stomach, and this provides faster pain relief than taking ibuprofen with food. Food slows ibuprofen absorption time, although it doesn't affect the total amount absorbed. There is actually no scientific evidence that taking ibuprofen with food prevents stomach irritation. Over-the-counter ibuprofen doses have a low incidence of gastric problems anyway.

raw_sentence: Q: Does Losartan block COVID-19 Coronavirus Receptors?
raw_line: Q: Does Losartan block COVID-19 Coronavirus Receptors? A: Losartan (Cozaar) does not directly block SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus receptors, but this angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB), may influence COVID-19 outcomes through its effects on the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Losartan works by blocking angiotensin II from binding to angiotensin II type 1 receptors (AT1) in the heart, blood vessels, kidneys, and lungs, reducing the activity of RAAS, which lowers blood pressure and may modulate the inflammatory response.

raw_line: In the landmark Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), a randomized controlled trial in people at high risk for diabetes, participants taking metformin lost more weight than those on placebo. raw_sentence: Q: Can you take ondansetron while pregnant?
raw_line: Q: Can you take ondansetron while pregnant? A: Although ondansetron is not specifically approved by the FDA to treat nausea and vomiting during pregnancy (NVP), its use is common, and approximately 25% of pregnant women are prescribed ondansetron to treat NVP. Overall, studies show the use of ondansetron appears to be associated with an additional 3 instances of oral cleft defects (such as cleft lip or cleft palate) for every 10,000 women exposed to ondansetron during their first trimester. There may also be a very slight increased risk of a type of heart defect called a ventricular septal defect, but no apparent increased risk of other birth defects, miscarriage, or fetal death.

A: Pantoprazole starts to work within 2 and a half (2.5) hours – this is the time it takes for it to block the secretion of acid in the stomach - and lasts for 24 hours. Pantoprazole does not provide fast-acting relief from indigestion, acid reflux, or dyspepsia symptoms like antacids such as Tums or Maalox do, and will not treat current symptoms. It may take up to 4 weeks for pantoprazole to work properly so you may still have some symptoms during this time.

raw_sentence: Q: Pantoprazole vs. omeprazole: What's the difference between them?
raw_line: Q: Pantoprazole vs. omeprazole: What's the difference between them? A: Pantoprazole and omeprazole are both proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) that reduce stomach acid and show similar effectiveness for healing acid‑related conditions such as erosive esophagitis. Their main differences relate to FDA‑approved uses, availability (omeprazole is OTC; pantoprazole is prescription), timing with food, and the option for intravenous (IV) pantoprazole in the hospital setting.

raw_sentence: Q: Can you take pantoprazole 40 mg twice a day?
raw_line: Q: Can you take pantoprazole 40 mg twice a day? A: The usual dosage for pantoprazole 40mg is 40mg once a day if you are buying it without a prescription or a physician's evaluation of your symptoms. The only conditions that pantoprazole 40mg twice a day is recommended for are those characterized by excessively high gastric acid secretion such as Zollinger Ellison syndrome, and if you have these conditions then you should be under the care of a physician. Studies have shown that for reflux, dyspepsia, or GERD, dosages higher than 40mg did not offer any further significant lowering of stomach acid than 40mg dosages.

raw_sentence: Q: How long can I take pantoprazole?
raw_line: Q: How long can I take pantoprazole? A: You should only take pantoprazole for up to 8 weeks if you are buying it without a prescription or a physician evaluation of your symptoms. This is because certain stomach symptoms that persist for more than 4 to 8 weeks should be investigated by a doctor, as they may be a sign of something more serious, such as cancer. Pantoprazole is very good at relieving and hiding serious stomach symptoms, which may make you think you don’t need to see a physician. Long-term use of pantoprazole has also been associated with vitamin B12 deficiency; low magnesium, calcium, iron, or vitamin C levels; and an increased risk of fractures of the hip, wrist, or spine. Elderly, the malnourished, or those on dialysis are more at risk.

raw_sentence: Q: Does pantoprazole cause bloating?
raw_line: Q: Does pantoprazole cause bloating? A: Bloating has been reported as a side effect of regular pantoprazole use. One study reported bloating in 43% of patients taking a similar proton pump inhibitor to pantoprazole (called esomeprazole) after 8 weeks. By 6 months, over 50% reporting bloating. Other similar side effects reported with pantoprazole that also can have bloating as a side effect include flatulence, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. Symptoms of bloating include tightness, fullness, or swelling of your stomach area.

raw_line: Effects reported after a sertraline tablet overdose include seizures, which may be delayed, and changes in mental state including coma. raw_line: Q: Do statins cause rhabdomyolysis, and how is it treated? A: Rhabdomyolysis is a rare but serious side effect of statins, a class of cholesterol-lowering medications. While statins are generally safe, rhabdomyolysis from statins is uncommon and most likely to occur at high doses or when combined with certain other drugs.

raw_sentence: Some people are “ultra-rapid metabolizers” of tramadol because of a variation in an enzyme called CYP2D6.
raw_line: Some people are “ultra-rapid metabolizers” of tramadol because of a variation in an enzyme called CYP2D6. Their bodies convert tramadol into its active form faster than usual, which can produce dangerously high opioid levels even at a normal dose. Life-threatening breathing problems and deaths have occurred in children for this reason, including after surgery to remove the tonsils or adenoids.
